"title": "Environmentally friendly and roll-processed flexible organic solar cells based on PM6:Y6",

"type_of_paper": "Experimental study (pre-print)",
"executive_summary": "This pre-print reports the first open-air, roll-to-roll-compatible fabrication of flexible organic solar cells (OSCs) based on the high-efficiency PM6:Y6 non-fullerene blend using slot-die coating and a green solvent. The central motivation is to narrow the \"lab-to-fab gap\" that separates record lab-scale efficiencies from industrially scalable manufacturing. Spin-coating, the dominant lab technique, is criticized for poor upscaling potential and substantial material waste, whereas slot-die coating is preferred because it enables one-dimensional stripe patterning with almost no material waste and is compatible with roll-to-roll production. The authors coat the PM6:Y6 active layer using o-xylene (O-XY), a green solvent with ≥ 98% purity, without additives, and heat the substrate, syringe, tube, and slot-die head to keep the temperature-dependent-aggregating (TDA) PM6 liquid during coating. The optimal coating temperature is identified as 100 °C, where power conversion efficiency (PCE) saturates and bimolecular recombination is minimized (S = 0.978). Ternary devices with PC61BM and fully printed devices are also fabricated, achieving average PCEs of 6.6% and 6.7% respectively, with a champion efficiency of 7.2% for the ternary device. The study demonstrates that a small amount of fullerene acceptor enhances exciton dissociation (93.7% binary vs. 96.3% and 95.7% for ternary blends) and charge collection (69.6% binary vs. 77.7% and 73.2% for ternary blends). Devices are fabricated on pre-patterned ITO-coated PET substrates with an inverted ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag geometry, with active areas of approximately 0.8 cm². Remarkably, the devices exhibit exceptional stability, retaining 99.4% of their initial PCE after 1050 hours of dark storage for the ternary device and more than 97% for binary devices after more than 1500 hours. The authors argue that these results pave the way for upscaling OSC production based on the PM6:Y6 system, bringing the technology closer to commercialization. The study is notable for its environmental focus, using a green solvent without additives, and its demonstration of the feasibility of slot-die coating on flexible substrates in open air. The results are supported by comprehensive characterization, including J-V curves, external quantum efficiency (EQE) measurements, absorbance spectra, and light intensity dependence studies to probe recombination mechanisms. The paper concludes that matching the flexible substrate temperature with the hot slot-die head at 100 °C maximizes PCE due to reduced bimolecular recombination, and that the optimal active layer thickness is around 200 nm. The authors acknowledge that the devices are not prepared in a cleanroom or inside a glovebox, which explains the high degree of trap-assisted recombination observed under open-circuit conditions. This limitation is important because it suggests that further efficiency improvements may be possible under more controlled conditions. Overall, the study makes a significant contribution to the field of scalable organic photovoltaics by demonstrating that high-efficiency PM6:Y6 devices can be fabricated using environmentally friendly and roll-processed methods, with excellent stability that could be attractive for commercial applications.",

summary.title: Environmentally friendly and roll-processed flexible organic solar cells based on PM6:Y6
summary.authors: Marcial Fernández Castro, Jean Truer, Espíndola Rodríguez, Jens Wenzel
summary.executive_summary: This pre-print reports the first open-air, roll-to-roll-compatible fabrication of flexible organic solar cells (OSCs) based on the high-efficiency PM6:Y6 non-fullerene blend using slot-die coating and a green solvent. The central motivation is to narrow the "lab-to-fab gap" that separates record lab-scale efficiencies from industrially scalable manufacturing. Spin-coating, the dominant lab technique, is criticized for poor upscaling potential and substantial material waste, whereas slot-die coating is preferred because it enables one-dimensional stripe patterning with almost no material waste and is compatible with roll-to-roll production. The authors coat the PM6:Y6 active layer using o-xylene (O-XY), a green solvent with ≥ 98% purity, without additives, and heat the substrate, syringe, tube, and slot-die head to keep the temperature-dependent-aggregating (TDA) PM6 liquid during coating. The optimal coating temperature is identified as 100 °C, where power conversion efficiency (PCE) saturates and bimolecular recombination is minimized (S = 0.978). Ternary devices with PC61BM and fully printed devices are also fabricated, achieving average PCEs of 6.6% and 6.7% respectively, with a champion efficiency of 7.2% for the ternary device. The study demonstrates that a small amount of fullerene acceptor enhances exciton dissociation (93.7% binary vs. 96.3% and 95.7% for ternary blends) and charge collection (69.6% binary vs. 77.7% and 73.2% for ternary blends). Devices are fabricated on pre-patterned ITO-coated PET substrates with an inverted ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag geometry, with active areas of approximately 0.8 cm². Remarkably, the devices exhibit exceptional stability, retaining 99.4% of their initial PCE after 1050 hours of dark storage for the ternary device and more than 97% for binary devices after more than 1500 hours. The authors argue that these results pave the way for upscaling OSC production based on the PM6:Y6 system, bringing the technology closer to commercialization. The study is notable for its environmental focus, using a green solvent without additives, and its demonstration of the feasibility of slot-die coating on flexible substrates in open air. The results are supported by comprehensive characterization, including J-V curves, external quantum efficiency (EQE) measurements, absorbance spectra, and light intensity dependence studies to probe recombination mechanisms. The paper concludes that matching the flexible substrate temperature with the hot slot-die head at 100 °C maximizes PCE due to reduced bimolecular recombination, and that the optimal active layer thickness is around 200 nm. The authors acknowledge that the devices are not prepared in a cleanroom or inside a glovebox, which explains the high degree of trap-assisted recombination observed under open-circuit conditions. This limitation is important because it suggests that further efficiency improvements may be possible under more controlled conditions. Overall, the study makes a significant contribution to the field of scalable organic photovoltaics by demonstrating that high-efficiency PM6:Y6 devices can be fabricated using environmentally friendly and roll-processed methods, with excellent stability that could be attractive for commercial applications.

claims.description: Slot-die coating is a scalable fabrication technique that can be used to fabricate high-efficiency PM6:Y6 OSCs on flexible substrates in open air with a green solvent.
The optimal coating temperature of 100 °C maximizes PCE due to reduced bimolecular recombination.
The addition of a small amount of fullerene acceptor improves PCE and stability in open-air flexible devices.
The devices exhibit exceptional stability under dark storage, retaining over 99% of the initial efficiency.

The optimal coating temperature is identified as 100 °C, where power conversion efficiency (PCE) saturates and bimolecular recombination is minimized (S = 0.978). Ternary devices with PC61BM and fully printed devices are also fabricated, achieving average PCEs of 6.6% and 6.7% respectively, with a champion efficiency of 7.2% for the ternary device. The study demonstrates that a small amount of fullerene acceptor enhances exciton dissociation (93.7% binary vs. 96.3% and 95.7% for ternary blends) and charge collection (69.6% binary vs. 77.7% and 73.2% for ternary blends). Devices are fabricated on pre-patterned ITO-coated PET substrates with an inverted ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag geometry, with active areas of approximately 0.8 cm². Remarkably, the devices exhibit exceptional stability, retaining 99.4% of their initial PCE after 1050 hours of dark storage for the ternary device and more than 97% for binary devices after more than 1500 hours. The authors argue that these results pave the way for upscaling OSC production based on the PM6:Y6 system, bringing the technology closer to commercialization. The study is notable for its environmental focus, using a green solvent without additives, and its demonstration of the feasibility of slot-die coating on flexible substrates in open air. The results are supported by comprehensive characterization, including J-V curves, external quantum efficiency (EQE) measurements, absorbance spectra, and light intensity dependence studies to probe recombination mechanisms. The paper concludes that matching the flexible substrate temperature with the hot slot-die head at 100 °C maximizes PCE due to reduced bimolecular recombination, and that the optimal active layer thickness is around 200 nm. The authors acknowledge that the devices are not prepared in a cleanroom or inside a glovebox, which explains the high degree of trap-assisted recombination observed under open-circuit conditions. This limitation is important because it suggests that further efficiency improvements may be possible under more controlled conditions. Overall, the study makes a significant contribution to the field of scalable organic photovoltaics by demonstrating that high-efficiency PM6:Y6 devices can be fabricated using environmentally friendly and roll-processed methods, with excellent stability that could be attractive for commercial applications.

Research Context
Organic solar cells (OSCs) have reached high efficiencies using non-fullerene acceptors that allow fine-tuning of energy levels and light absorption. OSCs offer low cost, mechanical flexibility, lightweight properties, semi-transparency, and very short Energy Payback Time (EPBT). A large efficiency gap remains between lab-scale devices and those produced using industry-compatible processes. Slot-die coating is preferred for scalable fabrication due to one-dimensional patterning and minimal material waste. The PM6:Y6 material combination has shown excellent efficiencies over 15% on rigid substrates using green solvents. There is a need to transfer PM6:Y6 devices to roll-processing on flexible substrates using scalable fabrication techniques. PM6 exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation (TDA) behavior, requiring heating to remain liquid during coating.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can high-efficiency PM6:Y6 OSCs be fabricated using slot-die coating on flexible substrates in open air with a green solvent? What is the optimal coating temperature for maximizing PCE while minimizing recombination? How does active layer thickness affect device performance and stability? Can adding a small amount of fullerene acceptor improve PCE and stability in open-air flexible devices? Will slot-die coated flexible devices exhibit good stability under dark storage? The authors hypothesize that coating at 100 °C will maximize PCE due to reduced bimolecular recombination. The authors predict that the optimal active layer thickness is around 200 nm for high performance. The authors expect that adding PC61BM will enhance exciton dissociation and charge collection.

Methodological Details
The study used PM6 (batch YY19260CH100) and Y6 (batch DW7038S) purchased from 1-Material Inc. PB61BM (batch M111) was purchased from Ossila for use as a fullerene acceptor. ZnO nanoparticle ink was from Sigma-Aldrich and MoO3 pellets from Kurt J. Lesker Co. The flexible substrate was pre-patterned ITO-coated PET purchased from FOM Technologies. Pure silver was bought from Sigma-Aldrich for back electrode evaporation. Silver paste for flexographic printing was a heat-curing paste (DuPont 5025). The solvent used was O-XY with ≥ 98% purity purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Materials were purchased and used directly without purification. The device used an inverted geometry of ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag. The ZnO ETL was coated at 75 °C with a 0.06 mL/min flow rate and 1.08 m/min drum speed. The ZnO ETL was annealed in an oven at 100 °C for 10 min in air. The AL PM6:Y6 was coated at a 1:1 ratio with concentrations from 12 to 28 mg/mL. The AL was coated at temperatures of 60, 80, 100, and 120 °C. The drum speed was kept at 1.5 m/min with a 0.12 mL/min flow rate. 10 nm of MoO3 and 150 nm of Ag were thermally evaporated under vacuum. Evaporation was performed at a base pressure of 2 x 10^-5 mbar through a shadow mask. Up to 24 solar cells were fabricated per evaporation from a one-meter-long AL. At least 8 devices were encapsulated with an active area of approximately 0.8 cm². The devices had an approximate active area of 0.8 cm². An activation process applied a reverse bias current of -5 V with a maximum current of 100 mA. Encapsulation used epoxy-based glue EPXR made of bisphenol A diglycidyl ether and Chissonox 221 monomers. Curing was made under UV light for approximately 5 min reaching 66 ± 0.5 °C. J-V curves were measured with a Keithley 2400 source meter with a 50 mV step. The solar simulator was calibrated to 1000 W/m² with a monocrystalline silicon reference cell. A shadow mask from Ossila (E2002A1) defined an aperture area of 0.3996 cm². Averages included statistics of eight devices. EQE and absorbance were measured with a QEX10 system from 300 to 1100 nm. Light intensity was increased from 62.14 mW/cm² to 147.33 mW/cm² for recombination studies. Thickness measurements were done with a DS95-50 AFM instrument in noncontact mode. The AFM scan dimension was a 5 × 5 µm² surface.

Procedures And Architectures
A homemade roll-coater was fabricated to coat under fully compatible roll-to-roll conditions at laboratory scale. A syringe pump controlled the flow rate of the inks. The setup controlled the speed and heat of the drum and the drum-to-head distance. A hot tube was necessary to bring the AL from the syringe to the slot-die head. The head, syringe, drum, and tube were kept at the same temperature for each temperature under investigation. The AL was coated at different temperatures and concentrations to study the effect. The materials were sequentially evaporated from different tungsten boats. An INFICON XTM/2 system was used to monitor the deposition rate and thickness. Different parts of the AL were selected to fabricate solar cells before encapsulation. The coating temperature optimization was performed first, then the effect of AL thickness. The D/A ratio was fixed at 1:1 as the highest reported efficiencies were achieved with that ratio. The coating temperature was screened from 60 °C to 120 °C matching with the drum and tube temperature. The absorption of PM6 in dried films was the same for different coating temperatures. Annealing at 120 °C for 3 minutes improved JSC of devices with AL coated at 60 °C and 80 °C. Devices fabricated at 100 °C and 120 °C did not improve after annealing. The EQE increased with higher coating temperatures, indicating better carrier collection. The short-circuit current was higher at higher coating temperatures. The average FF value was 42.2% for the 120 °C coating versus 47.10% for the 100 °C coating. The PCE showed a clear improvement trend towards higher coating temperature saturating around 100 °C. The S value closest to unity (S = 0.978) was obtained by coating at 100 °C. The slope values were higher than kT/q, suggesting trap-assisted recombination as the dominant mechanism. Four different AL thicknesses were investigated to study the effect on efficiency. The absorption peaks of both materials were distinguished with donor maximum at ~625 nm. The highest PCE obtained in the thickness optimization was 6.3% with an FF of 49.0%. The average PCE for the 217 nm AL thickness was 5.8%. The JSC reached its maximum at 154 nm of AL thickness (17.3 mA/cm²). The FF improved from 42.0% for the thinnest AL to 47.1% for 116 nm AL. The ternary blend started with a [1:1:0.2] ratio. The amount of PC61BM was reduced by half to a [1:1.1:0.1] ratio. Short current circuit values of up to 20 mA/cm² were measured on ternary blend devices. A 12% higher JSC was obtained from the [1:1:0.2] ternary blend compared with binary devices. The average PCE of the [1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1] ternary devices were 6.6% and 6.7% respectively. The collection probability improved from 69.6% for the binary device to 77.7% and 73.2% for ternary devices. The dissociation probability was 93.7% for the binary device versus 96.3% and 95.7% for ternary blends. The stability was determined by measuring encapsulated devices after storage in dark following the ISOS-D-1 protocol. The average PCEs measured after 1050 hours for the ternary device retained 99.4% of the initial value. The average PCEs of binary devices retained more than 97% after more than 1500 hours. The optimal coating temperature was fixed at 100 °C based on higher PCE and ease of coating.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The optimal coating temperature of 100 °C maximizes PCE due to reduced bimolecular recombination. Coating at higher temperatures induces better carrier collection, thus a higher current. The aggregation of materials on both edges of the AL at temperatures above 100 °C creates inhomogeneities. The inhomogeneities along the stripe directly impact the fill factor of the final devices. The trap-assisted recombination is the dominant mechanism due to impurities in the materials. The high degree of trap-assisted recombination is expected because devices are not prepared in a cleanroom. The addition of PC61BM enhances exciton dissociation possibly due to additional energetically favorable interfaces. The energy cascade effect of PC61BM is favorable to obtain enhanced values of JSC and VOC. The small amount of ternary compound has a positive effect on the current and the FF. The better charge extraction can be achieved with a small acceptor fullerene amount in OSCs on flexible substrates. The exceptional stability suggests that the devices could be attractive for commercial applications. The results demonstrate that high-efficiency PM6:Y6 devices can be fabricated using environmentally friendly methods. The demonstration paves the way for upscaling the production of OSCs based on the PM6:Y6 system. The study shows that slot-die coating can be transferred to a roll-to-roll platform. The study contributes to reducing the lab-to-fab gap and bringing the technology closer to commercialization.

Contradictions And Limitations
The devices are not prepared in a cleanroom or inside a glovebox, explaining the high trap-assisted recombination. The high degree of trap-assisted recombination may limit further efficiency improvements.
